title: Three Words From Cairo
hook: Her telegram home was three words long: *Oswald in His presence.*
dateline: Oswald Chambers · Died on this day, November 15, 1917 · Cairo, Egypt
summary: On November 15, 1917, Oswald Chambers died in Cairo at 43. His widow's shorthand became My Utmost for His Highest.

lead_image.alt: Rows of white headstones at the Cairo War Memorial Cemetery, where Oswald Chambers is buried

story: The telegram Biddy Chambers sent home to England was three words long: "Oswald in His presence." Her husband had died in a Cairo hospital at about seven that morning, November 15, 1917, 109 years ago today. He was 43.

For two years Oswald Chambers had served as a YMCA chaplain to soldiers in Egypt during the First World War, most of that time at Zeitoun, a desert army camp on the edge of Cairo. Australian, New Zealand and British troops passed through. He had asked to bring his wife and their toddler, Kathleen, and the surprised YMCA agreed. He preached most nights. Biddy, who had trained as a stenographer, sat with a notebook and took down his talks in shorthand.

He hadn't always been this sure of God. Born in Aberdeen, Scotland, in 1874, he trained as an artist in London and Edinburgh before sensing, at about 22, that God was calling him to preach instead. The years that followed at Dunoon College in Scotland were full of spiritual struggle, until a turning point in 1901.

In October 1917 sharp pain set in low in his side. Wounded men were coming back from the fighting in Palestine, and he refused to take a hospital bed one of them might need. By the time surgeons removed his appendix on October 29, he was gravely ill. He seemed to recover. Then, in early November, a blood clot set off bleeding in his lungs, and on November 15 he died.

The soldiers gave him a military funeral through old Cairo, and about 100 men escorted the gun carriage that carried his coffin. He was buried in what is now the Cairo War Memorial Cemetery, under the words "A believer in Jesus Christ."

Here is the strange part. Chambers proofread only one book of his own: *Baffled to Fight Better*, a set of talks on Job that he proofread before he fell ill. It came out in December, after his death. Everything else bearing his name came from Biddy's shorthand. Widowed in her early thirties, with a four-year-old, she stayed in Egypt and ran the camp's work until the war ended, mailing his talks to soldiers as pamphlets. Back in England she spent the rest of her life turning his talks into books.

In 1927 she published 365 short daily readings pulled from those notes, titled *My Utmost for His Highest*. It has never gone out of print. The Oswald Chambers Publications Association now lists translations in 45 languages.
His name is on the cover. Her pencil is on every page. And the God who could have healed him chose instead to keep his voice going through a widow's notebook, one morning at a time.

quote.text: Shut out every other consideration and keep yourself before God for this one thing only—"My Utmost for His Highest."
quote.source: Oswald Chambers, My Utmost for His Highest (1927), "Let Us Keep to the Point"

scripture.text: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
scripture.note: Biddy asked for this psalm to be sung at his graveside.

why: Oswald Chambers never saw the book that made his name. A widow's shorthand did that. *My Utmost for His Highest* has stayed in print for almost a century, and people still open it every morning, in dozens of languages. God doesn't waste a voice cut short, or the faithful person quietly writing it down.
